summary: West Virginia does not tie smoke alarms to a sale, but it puts a standing duty on the owner of every one- and two-family home to have a working smoke detector near each sleeping area, so a seller's house has to have them anyway.
alarmType: A working smoke detector in the immediate vicinity of each sleeping area in every one- and two-family dwelling, including a manufactured home. It must be able to sense visible or invisible particles of combustion, must meet the specifications in the current edition of the State Fire Code and be installed as that code and the manufacturer's instructions provide, and must sound an alarm loud enough to warn occupants. The statute names no power source for smoke detectors. An automatic fire sprinkler system installed to the current State Fire Code and State Building Code may be used instead of smoke detectors. Where a non-owner-occupied dwelling is occupied by someone deaf or hard of hearing, the owner must provide a detector with a light signal on written request.
coAlarms: Treated separately and not tied to sale. A working single-station CO detector, or a combination smoke/CO detector, must be AC powered - either plugged into an outlet not controlled by a switch, or hardwired to an AC source - with battery backup, and installed and maintained per the manufacturer's directions. It is required in a newly constructed residential unit with a fuel-burning heating or cooking source; in a residential unit connected to a newly constructed building (garage, shed, barn) with such a source; and in apartment buildings, boarding houses, dormitories, long-term care, adult or child care, assisted living, hotels, motels, and one- and two-family dwellings intended to be rented or leased, in a common public area or in all sleeping rooms adjoining and directly above or below areas with permanently installed fuel-burning appliances. In newly constructed buildings of those types the detector must be hardwired with battery backup. An existing owner-occupied one- or two-family home is not covered by the CO provisions.
certification: No inspection or certificate at sale. Enforcement is after the fact: following a fire, the local investigating authority must issue the owner a smoke detector installation order if the required detectors were missing. Violating the section is a misdemeanor with fines of $250, $750, and $2,000 for first, second, and later offenses. A violation is not evidence of negligence in a civil case and is not a defense in an insurance proceeding. Anyone installing a CO detector must tell the owner, lessor, or occupant about CO dangers and how to operate it, and anyone doing repair or maintenance on a fuel-burning heating or cooking source or venting system in an existing residential unit must warn of CO dangers and recommend a CO detector.
citation: W. Va. Code § 15A-10-12 (formerly § 29-3-16a, which is now repealed)
lastAmended: 2020 (Enrolled Committee Substitute for S.B. 586, 2020 Regular Session), which moved the section from § 29-3-16a to § 15A-10-12
notVerified: The absence of a sale/transfer rule is based on a full-code search of code.wvlegislature.gov for "smoke detector," which returned 43 sections; the only residential alarm sections are § 15A-10-12 and the repealed § 29-3-16a. Nothing in the property or conveyance chapters came up.

The detector specifications themselves are in the State Fire Code (a State Fire Commission legislative rule in Title 87 CSR) rather than the statute; that rule was not read, so the required listing standard, placement details, and whether a sealed 10-year battery is acceptable were not verified.
Local political subdivisions are expressly allowed to impose a greater duty than the statute, and no local ordinance was checked.
